claims.text: A modified TILD workflow can combine solid- and liquid-phase sampling, reweighting, and machine-learning interatomic potentials trained on sparse ab initio reference data.
The proposed workflow will substantially reduce the cost of calculating solid–liquid free energies and fusion properties in multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The workflow will retain vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration contributions in both solid and liquid phases.
Near-equimolar quaternary and quinary alloys such as AlCoFeNi and CoCrFeMnNi variants are within the intended composition domain.
Interatomic-potential simulations can reproduce selected first-principles and experimental properties of a multicomponent high-entropy alloy.
Sparse ab initio training data are sufficient to produce an accurate machine-learning potential for solid and liquid states near melting.
Periodic ab initio corrections will preserve ab initio-level fidelity during ML-potential sampling.
The ML-based potential can accurately represent vibrational entropy, anharmonic effects, and electron–vibration coupling.
TILD-based integration with a surrogate potential will sample the computationally expensive melting region more efficiently than explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed method will provide an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational time relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics or standard TOR-TILD.
Calculated free energies, fusion enthalpies, and heat capacities will agree within approximately 5–10% of full ab initio benchmarks.
Existing TOR-TILD approaches have been validated on elemental or binary systems and become computationally expensive for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Extreme composition ratios, large atomic-size mismatch, or unanticipated short-range order may require additional reference data or alternative sampling.
Sampling from below the solidus to several hundred kelvin above melting will permit thermodynamic characterization of both solid and fluid regions.
The benchmark should cover temperatures from 100 K below to 200 K above the melting point of a selected quinary alloy.
A discrepancy greater than approximately 10% in phase free energies or derived thermodynamic quantities will falsify the hypothesis.
